paragraphs.text: Truly the grace of Christ has appeared to us, and with it the power of godliness has shone out upon us. Truly the sun of righteousness has risen upon us, and the ends of the earth bear witness that they have been enlightened. For the Lord of the heavens has appeared, and, as he willed, he has made the whole earth into heaven, as was said to you before. Being heavenly, he makes people heavenly, and he bestows heavenly gifts on those who are heavenly. From the Faithful One come faithful gifts to the faithful; from the Holy One, holy gifts to the holy; from the Living One, living gifts to the living. These are the things we set before you in the sacred and royal courts of the apostles, when we touched on the meaning of the prophets, when heaven and earth divided the voices of the prophets between them. The earth had John, saying, "A voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight"; and heaven had the voice of the Father, confirmed by deeds: "The voice of the Lord is upon the waters."

These are the things we put before you. They are enough to remind the diligent and to strengthen the faithful. But you should know that going over good things again makes your souls more steadfast. We see that the earth is best cultivated when it is worked with the same ploughs, and a second ploughing goes over the first surface and makes it fine. In the same way, when the soul has been ploughed by the divine word, and the memory of what was said before comes in and renews the mind, it makes the soul more fertile in bearing the fruit of virtue.

Now it is time for us to pay our debt, a debt that we ourselves promised and that you keep in mind. I ask all who love Christ to lend both their ears and their minds, so that the ear may take in what is said without missing anything, and the mind may examine its meaning carefully. For our subject is Christ. Everything said about Christ is not a simple proclamation but a mystery of godliness. The whole dispensation of Christ is called a mystery. A mystery is not seen in the letter; it is proclaimed in the reality. That is why Scripture calls the whole dispensation of Christ a mystery, as when Paul says, "This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the church"; and again, "Beyond question, great is the mystery of godliness, which was revealed in the flesh"; and again, "The mystery was made known to me by revelation, as you can perceive when you read, understanding my insight into the mystery of Christ"; and elsewhere, "To me, the very least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to you the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to bring to light for all what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages and from the generations, but now revealed to his saints, to whom God willed to make known what are the riches of the glory of his mystery among the nations, which is Christ, the hope of glory."

So the children of heretics go astray when they subject the mystery of God to human reasoning. For he says, "My mystery is for me and for those who are mine." And who are God's own? Clearly, the faithful. When you want to learn or hear something about Christ, do not consult reasoning, do not question a wise man. Ask a prophet, ask an apostle, question an angel. And if they are at a loss, run to the Father.

If you ask the prophets, "Who is this Christ?", the chorus of prophets answers you: "This is our God; no other shall be compared with him. He found out every way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel whom he loved. Afterward he appeared on earth and lived among human beings." But if you ask, "Who is this Christ, and how was he begotten?", prying into the divine birth, the prophets stop your bold mouth and begin to say: "What our reasoning could not grasp, can you grasp? If you want to learn, learn that he is God. But if you are prying into how he was begotten, learn from us: 'Who shall declare his generation?'"

If you ask an apostle—I mean the chorus of apostles—they will tell you that Christ is God: God in the beginning, God with God, and God for ever. They will tell you: "The radiance of his glory and the exact imprint of his being, the image of the invisible God, upholding all things by the word of his power." If you ask, "How was he who is begotten?", they will tell you: "We have heard the word 'was', and we have learned that he was. But how he who is comes from him who is, we have received by faith, not by comprehension." And if you ask them again, "If you do not know how he was begotten, how do you know that he is the Son of God?", they will tell you: "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth."

Again, if you leave the apostles and the prophets and run to the angels and say to them, "Who is this Christ who is being proclaimed?", those who brought the good news to the shepherds will tell you: "We have learned to glorify, not to pry. 'Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men.' This is how we proclaim him: 'We bring you good news of great joy, which shall be for all the people: for to you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, who is Christ the Lord.' That he is Christ, and that he is Savior and Lord, we know." But if you say to them, "Tell us what his nature is, or how he was begotten, or how his power is undivided from the Father," they will tell you: "Have you not heard the prophet saying, 'Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise him in the heights; praise him, all his angels; praise him, all his hosts, his ministers who do his will'? We have been commanded to do his will, not to pry into his nature."

But perhaps, while the angels keep silent, the prophets do not tell, and the apostles hold back, the Father who begot him proclaims how he begot the Son? Not even he—not because he does not know, but because he does not disclose it. That he begot him, he does say: "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you." He says that he begot him, and he does not hide that immortal offspring which blossomed from the eternal root, as the Father bears witness about him, saying, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." To him he says, "From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you"; to the world he says, "I have begotten." He declares the nature, but he does not explain the manner.

Since, then, we have before us a necessary inquiry about Christ, let us not go beyond the springs of the prophets and apostles. Let us draw the divine streams of inspired teaching from those ever-flowing currents and immortal rivers. For when someone speaks the things of God from the things of God, he draws living streams as from a living spring, as it is written: "They have forsaken me, the spring of living water"; and again, "Drink water from the springs of salvation." But if we abandon the Scriptures and become slaves to the desires of human reasoning, thinking whatever reasoning suggests, the waters of our teaching turn out to be desert waters—not of a living river, but of the desert. As blessed Jeremiah said to Jerusalem, "She widened her ways toward the waters of the desert." And to explain what he means, he adds, "She was carried along by the desires of her soul"—that is, she spoke what her soul desired, not what God willed. So too now, whoever fulfills the desires of his own reasoning and does not seek the things of God wanders off toward desert waters. Nothing destroys the beauty of the church so much as giving authority to the desires of human reasoning. That is why Paul said of the heretics, "In keeping with their own desires they heap up teachers for themselves."

Let us come, then, to the debt. We have had to give you, my beloved, this word in advance, so that you may seek a careful examination of everything that is said, not from us and our own reasonings but from the divine Scriptures. We had undertaken to show how Christ renews the world: how Christ, through his own dispensation, renews the human being who had grown old in paradise through sin. We made this promise in the sacred courts of the apostles, but held back its fulfillment because not everyone was present.

Let us take a starting point that everyone agrees on and that suits our subject: the creation. God made heaven and earth. This is a fitting beginning for what is to be said: the first footing of the world, the first foundation of creation. God made heaven and earth and the sea and all that is in them—to put it briefly. Everything else he brought forth by a word. His command met no resistance; he endured no toil and suffered no sweat. The nature of created things simply followed upon his speaking.

He made the whole creation, and at the end, the crown of creation's beauty: the human being. For just as our whole body appears dead without the face, so all of visible creation is dead apart from the making of the human being. Listen how: the sun is bright, but it cannot explain itself. The moon is bright, but it did not teach its own phases; it was speech that handed them down.

The order of the stars is splendid, but it was teaching that handed down their rhythms. The sea is great, but it was the human tongue that described its gulfs. There is nothing that has come into being in the world that does not need the human voice to interpret it. This is what shows that something that seems unfitting is in fact good, and that what is good is truly good. For sight is often deceived and leads the mind astray; but speech comes in and shows the nature of a thing, points out its power, and explains its lesson.

Pay attention, then. God made the whole creation, and at the end of creation he fashioned the human being according to his own image and likeness. The image he granted was not the shape of the body but the dignity of rule, the power of discernment, and the capacity to become like the Maker through virtue.

So the human being came to be in the image and likeness of God; but he stretched that likeness beyond all measure. And do not think that this is foreign to the question before us, for what we are working through now is the root of what is to be said. He made the human being in his own image and likeness. He wanted him to press on toward resemblance to the Master's dignity—but with measure, in due sequence, and in order.

Let me explain, for we should also establish what we are investigating by everyday examples. If one of us, a master, has a slave and sees the slave imitating his self-control, he loves and honors him. If the slave imitates his master's kindness, the master loves his possession. If he sees his slave spending his time in church, devout, fasting, and giving alms, the master loves the slave's good imitation. But if the slave carries his imitation beyond measure and begins to imitate the master's authority—giving orders to his fellow slaves as if he were the master, squandering the property as if he were the master—then the imitation is no longer praiseworthy but blameworthy. For the slave ought to imitate his master's gentleness, self-control, piety, and justice, not his authority or his lordship.

So the human being, having received the ability to imitate God's goodness, stretched the measure of imitation beyond all measure and came to desire to rival God—not in virtue, but in authority. For this is how the serpent deceived him, saying, "On the day you eat, you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." God praises imitation when it keeps to its measure; but if it exceeds the measure, the imitator falls under blame. And where do we see this? He says, "Let us make man according to our image and likeness." The apostles became like God, and they were not reproached. The prophets became like God, and they were not blamed: they became imitators of his kindness, mercy, justice, and piety. But someone became like God in divine authority, and he was punished at once. Isaiah says to a certain tyrant in Babylon who in his madness claimed equality with God: "You said in your heart, 'I will ascend into heaven, and I will sit on the lofty mountains toward the north; I will ascend above the clouds, I will set my throne above the stars, and I will be like the Most High.' But now you will go down to Hades, to the foundations of the earth." Do you see how he punishes the one who is puffed up with pride?

For what objection could there be to his becoming like the Creator, if he had been made according to the image and likeness of the one who created him? But his boundless daring knew no measure in its likeness. He abandoned likeness in virtue and ran after likeness in the Master's authority. So also, in the case of David, he says, "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart." Here is likeness according to the image, since David's mind looked toward God: it was full of gentleness, brimming with humility, concerned for justice, and devoted to kindness. "I have found David the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart." The one who rightly imitated God's heart he praised; but another, a tyrant, who imitated God's heart not in virtue but in lordship, he condemned—or rather, he punished. And God says through Ezekiel: "And you, son of man, say to the ruler of Tyre: 'Because your heart was lifted up, and you said, "I am God" (though you are a man and not God), and you set your heart as the heart of God, therefore, behold, I will bring upon you foreigners, plagues from the nations, and they will draw their swords against you and against the beauty of your wisdom.'" And, to be brief, he adds: "You shall die the death of the slain in the heart of the sea. Will you still say, 'I am God,' in the presence of those who kill you?" Do you see how imitation without measure comes under punishment?

So the human being, having turned aside and slipped into a likeness without measure, found himself stripped even of what he had. For every mortal nature that desires what is beyond its power, against the will of God, not only gains nothing more but also loses what it has. Just as the eye rejoices and is enlightened when it enjoys a moderate ray of the sun, but if it tries to stare at the disk itself, it not only gains no more light but loses even what it has, so too mortal nature, desiring what is beyond its power against the will of God, has its mind darkened.

So the human being slipped, and from that slip many wounds followed upon the fall: idolatry, fornication, adultery, greed, and all their brothers and kin. The human being fell a very great fall, and through carelessness he lost the imprint of the divine countenance; for he was compared to the senseless beasts and became like them.

Then creation was divided: part of it threw off the reins, while part remained in service, as I said in the previous teaching. Lions plotted against the image; serpents bit; the whole nature of irrational creatures raged against its master. When it saw him counterfeit God's law, the rest of creation also wanted to escape his lordship. The sun wanted not to rise for the transgressor; the moon wanted to darken its rays; the stars wanted not to shine for the creature God had formed; the springs wanted to refuse their streams, the rivers their currents, the meadows their flowers, the gardens their delights. Everything wanted to reject the human being, since he had rejected his own Master. I know that this teaching is deep and shadowed, but for the sake of the faithful, those nurtured in the church, we must search out the meaning of divine Scripture. Creation served the human being not because he was worthy, but because God commanded that the image should not be utterly dishonored, even though it had transgressed.

So when the whole creation was in revolt, God commanded creation not to throw off the reins, but for the sun to give its ray, the earth its fruits, the sea its trade, and the stars their brightness. The apostle lays bare this very idea when he says, "For the eager longing of creation waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly, but because of him who subjected it, in hope that creation itself will also be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God."

Let me explain. When God saw that the human being had fallen and that creation was balking at serving the senseless one, he bridled it even against its will. He commanded the sun to rise and the earth to bear its fruits, and not to reject the transgressor for his ingratitude, but to display the Benefactor's ungrudging kindness. And he promised creation that it would be renewed together with the corrupted human being. It is as though God said to creation: "Since the image has fallen and slipped through transgression and is being corrupted through disobedience, bear with serving the corruption of the corrupted one, so that when I renew him—my image, my human being who has been corrupted—I may renew you, creation, along with him, and make you share the throne of his glory. You were dragged down with him in his misery; rise up with him in his glory."

And what does it mean, brother, that creation shuns the lordship of the human being? For it says, "Creation was subjected to futility." What futility? From the moment the human being turns away from God, he is called futility, as David says: "Surely all things are futility—every living man." Every human being who abandons God and pursues futile things is futile.

The angels, then, had been set over the nations throughout the whole earth, as Moses testifies, saying, "When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God." Let me explain: God assigned the regions of the world to each angel. For example, he allotted this province or that region to one angel, another to someone else, so that they might bridle this lifeless nature of sun and moon and stars and earth and sea for the enjoyment of mortal man. But again, the angels were worn down from serving unworthy human beings, and they were grieved to see the Master's dignity betrayed and idols worshiped. The angels were cut to the heart as they thought, "One is the giver, and others receive the thanks." The earth bore wine, and the altars received the libations; the earth bore an abundance of fruits, and they were offered to the idols. The angels could not bear the outrage of seeing things that are not honored in place of Him who Is.

This also resolves the other question, the one raised in the prophet. "The angel Gabriel came to him," it says, "and said to him: 'Daniel, servant of God, from the day you set yourself to afflict your soul before the Lord, your prayer was heard, and I was sent to announce these words to you. But the prince of the kingdom of the Persians withstood me, until Michael, the prince of your nation, came to my help.'" Who, then, is the angel who withstood Gabriel, and why did he withstand him?

It was said among you earlier too, brothers, that God assigned each of the angels a region, so that the whole creation would be guarded. So when holy Gabriel was sent from heaven, the angel set over the kingdom of the Persians, that is, over Persia, withstood him. The question is this: if that angel was sent by God, and Gabriel was also sent by God, why does he withstand him? If the angel who was sent belonged to another lord, he would be right to withstand him. But if it is the same God who set the one over the nation and sent the other to the prophet, why does he withstand him?

Pay close attention. The whole world was full of idolatry. The angels were indignant and distressed to see God set at nothing and idols worshiped. But when the people went down captive to Babylon, Daniel appeared, proclaiming God, and the three young men appeared, singing hymns to God. When the flame was trodden underfoot, impiety too was undone; when the lions were muzzled, the unbelievers too were silenced. So the angel who ruled the kingdom of the Persians rejoiced and leapt for joy that God was being proclaimed in his own regions. The angel saw the Chaldeans, who once worshiped fire and glorified idols, singing God's praises for the miracle. He rejoiced to see his own land, once thick with impiety, changed to piety. The angel saw King Nebuchadnezzar saying, "Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, servants of the Most High God," and he leapt for joy.

Blessed Daniel was praying to God that, now that the seventy appointed years were fulfilled, the people might be called back from captivity. Gabriel was sent to tell him that the people were being brought back from captivity and were about to take possession of their own land again, that is, Jerusalem. Then the angel withstood Gabriel, grieved that his land would once again be stripped of piety and filled with impiety. He grieved that his land would go back to its old state of idolatry, and so he withstood him, not by fighting but by pleading his case.

"Why are you so eager," he says, "to have the people called back? What harm did they suffer by being taken captive? When they were in their own land, they worshiped idols; since they came here, they glorify God. They have been helped themselves, and they have helped the people here. What stops them from staying among us? What wrong has the people suffered, that you are so eager to bring the captivity back? You see God worshiped and nations enlightened, and you hurry to undo so great a benefit? Why were you sent?" "I was sent," he says, "to bring the people back to their homeland." "What homeland?" he says. "The one they defiled with bloodshed when they lived in Jerusalem? Is this not what Jeremiah charges them with when he says, 'As many as your cities were your gods, O Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem you sacrificed to Baal'? Back then they received countless good things from God, and they did not turn away from wickedness. Now they suffer countless evils, and they do not turn away from God."

So this opposition was not evil set against good. Scripture did not say "he fought" but "he withstood." Often the just stands against the good. Sometimes mercy withstands the law, and the law withstands mercy. The law punishes the one who has sinned; a king's mercy pities the one who has sinned. So the struggle here is not of opposite against opposite, but of kin against kin. Justice is never found apart from goodness, and goodness is never found apart from justice.

But this has been said in passing; let us return to our subject. Such, then, was the state of creation: it was indignant at the transgressor, the angels were vexed at the ingratitude, and the whole world had been corrupted through lawlessness. For what a tree or any other material suffers, the earth suffers, as it is written: "And God saw the earth, and it was all corrupted, for all flesh had corrupted its way." He saw the earth, and it was corrupted. In this situation the prophets announced to the world the age to come, which would raise up the fallen world and renew the corrupted image.

And let no one suppose that my discourse makes many digressions because the thoughts move here and there. All of them lead back to a single point. Unless we first show how the world was corrupted, we cannot show how it was renewed.

So the whole earth was corrupted, the heaven dimmed, and all creation muddied. Creation was no longer as God had made it in the beginning. The heaven no longer shone with stars, the earth no longer abounded in fruit, the sea no longer in commerce. For the transgressor came in and defiled the earth. He defiled the heaven, the air, the sea, the springs, the rivers. He defiled everything with blasphemies: the heaven with blasphemy, the air with shameful words, the earth with unlawful bloodshed, the sea with pirates and robbers, the springs and the rivers with unlawful idolatries. For springs and rivers and gardens and trees and the whole creation were being made into gods. And nothing defiles creation so much as being made into a god.

So the whole creation was muddied. The Savior of the world comes in, or rather the apostles proclaim that he will come to renew all things. And not only the apostles: the prophets too foretold that Christ was coming. Why? So that no one would think that God, like a man, devises a second remedy when the first leaves him at a loss, moves on to a third when that one fails, and takes up a fourth when he misses with the third. To keep anyone from suspecting this, the prophets foretold the one who was to come. They wanted to show that God does not find out what is best by deliberating, but foresaw everything from the beginning. We human beings deliberate, and if our first attempt fails, we move on to another. God is not like that. He gave the law and the prophets, and after them the gospel. He did not learn over time what was best. He knew from the beginning that creation could not otherwise come to be and stand firm unless Christ appeared. When we human beings see diseases, that is when we think up remedies. But God, before our nature that he had formed was wounded, foresaw the medicine of salvation.

Many people say, "So God did not foreknow that Adam would sin?" My answer is that he not only foreknew this. Before the transgression he also foreknew that Christ would raise Adam up through the divine plan. He did not see the fall without having first planned the resurrection. He stored up the medicine of resurrection beforehand, and only then did he allow man to come to the experience of death, so that man might learn what he gets through himself and what he receives through God. In Egypt he first brought the years of plenty, storing them up beforehand as a remedy against the famine, and only then brought on the years of famine, so that the help of the medicine came before the wound. In the same way, before Adam was formed, before the lawless among his descendants appeared, before the righteous and the prophets among his descendants were born, God foresaw that this image could not stand firm unless Christ renewed it. In Adam God saw Paul; he saw Peter. He did not see Adam fed in paradise and about to be cast out. He saw in him Paul proclaiming true religion and caught up into paradise, and Peter entrusted with the keys of heaven. He saw everything in the first man, for the fruits were in the root.

Allow me for a little while to take part, as it were, in a conversation of God, and to bring God before you, as though by a kind of dramatic characterization, speaking with his own Son. And let no one think this way of speaking forced. When God made man, he used the Only-begotten as counselor and fellow worker: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." So it is reasonable that the Son also spoke to the Father. But wait for the end. Do not say, "This man is making guesses about God. He was not present at what happened there, so how does he know these things?" If the end does not match the meaning, judge me a slanderer.

"Let us make man in our image and likeness." He spoke as Creator; he answered as the one who knows beforehand: "If Adam sins, and he does sin, our workmanship will be blamed." Imagine either the Father saying these things to the Son or the Son to the Father. For there is no gap in the counsel of those whose essence is undivided. "But Adam sins, transgresses, dies; through him all human beings perish, and our handiwork is slandered as badly made." Then the counsel goes on: "But before all else we must settle the cure. You must, my Only-begotten, O Son, O Word, O radiance of my glory, you must, if you care at all for the handiwork we made by working together, put on the perishing man. You must take the apostles. Then, just as the devil used the serpent as his servant and his weapon for the deceit, you too will use your own handiwork as a servant for doing good, and will renew the fallen."

"But there will be many," he says, "who invent impious doctrines. The godless error of the Epicureans springs up. A heresy springs up that says human life is not governed by providence. Another heresy springs up that says the body is God. Many become teachers of error. Who, then, will undo these wicked things?"

I have said these things in a figure, so that at the end I may seal the meaning with the voice of the apostle. What, then? Must this garment that God the Word puts on run through all the ends of the earth under heaven and enlighten everyone? "No," he says, "but you will fulfill my divine plan. You will have the apostles as heralds of the divine Word. You will have Paul preaching. You will have Peter reaching Rome. You will have the apostles sharing in our plan."

These things were said before Adam was formed. First the things concerning Christ's flesh and the apostles were sketched out, and then Adam was formed. How do we know this? Listen to Paul saying, "The mystery hidden from the ages and the generations," and, "Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places, just as he chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, predestining us for adoption." And elsewhere he says about himself and those like him, "Those whom he foreknew to be conformed to the image of his Son." Paul was not only predestined and chosen. He also counts the grace he received many generations later as though he had received it before the ages. How do we know this? He says to Timothy, "Timothy, my child, share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and the grace given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages." He chose before the foundation of the world; he predestined before the ages; he gave us grace before the ages. All these agree that the Savior's plan was foreseen and predetermined before man was made.

But I know that I am speaking among friends of true religion, though sometimes also among spies. They pay no attention to the benefit of what is preached; they make it their one task to find how they can catch the speaker out. Truly, I do not hate their ways; I pity them instead. Still, in the words of the apostle, "because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who came in to spy out our freedom," let us examine the thought more closely. For an enemy could go out and say, "What grand theology! He brought in God deliberating and saying, 'Since many become teachers of error, what will happen?' And he had the Father speaking to the Son as though the Father were at a loss and the Son were teaching him these things."

When the Scriptures teach us about God, they never utter words fitted to the divine power, but words suited to our weakness. When God sets up a human court and says, "And now, you man of Judah and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard. What should I have done that I did not do?", is that the voice of one speaking or of one deliberating? And when he says to Isaiah, "Whom shall I send, and who will go to this people?", does he say it because he is in doubt, or because he does not know who his servant is? Whatever is said about God in the Church's teaching must be measured not by the power of the one who speaks but by the weakness of those who hear.

Our aim is to show that the things concerning Christ were prefigured before Adam, that the apostles were chosen beforehand, and that the grace of the gospel was prefigured before eternal ages. Pay close attention. A single word overlooked can fill what is said with slander.

In paradise God saw not only Adam transgressing but also the Savior, the Master who appeared in the flesh, opening the way to virtue and drawing everyone to obedience. God saw the side born out of Adam and changed into a woman, and he foresaw in turn the side of Christ bringing forth for us the mystical gifts, water and blood. The one is a symbol of the washing of baptism; the other is a pledge of the mysteries. And he did not so much lament the wound itself as call it blessed, considering the remedy.

There, woman came from man, leading to transgression; here, man came from woman, leading to salvation. There, a side gave birth to the cause of death; here, a side brings forth the pledge of incorruption. There, the serpent was at the tree; here, Christ is on the cross. There, food called forth death; here, food destroys death. You know the things of the faithful; recognize the mysteries. There, their eyes were opened for evil and they saw that they were naked; now our eyes are opened in true religion and we see that we are clothed. There, eyes opened and bodies stripped; here, illumination and clothing. There, garments of skin covered their shame; here, a garment of glory covers our weakness: the body of Christ, the robe of the King himself. For "as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ." There: "You are earth, and to earth you shall go." Here, having renewed the earth, he makes man heavenly, promising not earth but a kingdom. There, a flaming sword kept Adam out; here, tongues of fire from heaven enlighten Adam. There, he was cast out of paradise; here, he is entrusted with the keys of heaven.

God foresaw what was to come before what was present. Today, before we draw water, a channel is built for it, and before the waters flow the channel is called a waterway, not because water is flowing but because it is going to flow. In the same way God predetermined what was to be formed in Christ, and he knew that in Christ all things are renewed.

And he begins from above. He sets foot on heaven, as it is written: "Lord, bow your heavens and come down." He passed through the heavens, sanctifying them. He cut through the air to sanctify it, for it had been defiled by shameful songs. He treads the earth to sanctify it, for it had been polluted by murders. He walked on the waves of the sea to sanctify the waters that had been defiled. He is baptized in the Jordan to sanctify the nature of rivers. He also finds Adam lying in the tomb, takes on his image, and so Christ becomes both the one who comes after Adam and the renewal of Adam. Hear how. He takes up the form he had fashioned in paradise and adorns it with everything opposite, giving it the provisions of virtue, the reverse of the way of life in paradise. In paradise Adam was deceived through indulgence; Christ's flesh is crowned through fasting. In paradise came the first wrestling match; in the desert, the second contest against the devil.

So the Savior, renewing this handiwork, begins to crown it with every kind of virtue, and he comes in to mediate between God and human beings. He came to announce to the world that the fallen image is being renewed, raised up and saved. He could not have announced these things unless he were a mediator. For when a person of standing promises something to someone beneath him, the inferior does not dare to claim the promise unless he has a mediator [?]. Since God was invisible and the world was visible, he gives a trustworthy mediator. For "there is one mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ." A mediator who has no kinship with the parties between whom he mediates cannot be a mediator. So since Christ is "mediator between God and human beings," he had to be shown to be akin to God and akin to human beings, and to appear as a kind of middle dispensation, joined to God in his divinity and united to human beings in his humanity.

And what does he do? Since he first teaches and then renews, he becomes both mediator and guarantor. He conveys God's words to human beings and human beings' words to God. Because the human race had become hostile to God through the transgression, man did not trust God, nor did God trust man, that there would be reconciliation with the fallen. It is as if he said to human beings, "Do not refuse to believe that there is a resurrection. I am the guarantor of it. I take flesh from you and I hand it over to death. If I do not raise it, do not believe me." He stands guarantor to human beings for God. And it is as if he said, "Hold me answerable for man. I am renewing him; I will make him renounce error and acknowledge the truth. Accept me as guarantor for human beings, so that they too may accept me as guarantor of your power."

Scripture has shown that Christ is mediator. But where do we find that he is also guarantor and surety? We need to know, so that we do not appear to be speaking our own ideas in church. If I speak my own ideas, why speak at all? But if I proclaim the things of God, I am interpreting the things of the Spirit. Receive the teaching, then. That Christ is guarantor, Paul says: "But now we have obtained a more excellent ministry, just as Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant."

See: he stands guarantor to human beings for God. He guarantees both man to God and God to human beings. He said he would raise us, and he raises us. He said he would honor us with immortality, and he honors us. When he formed Adam, he gave no pledges for what he was doing and offered no guarantees, and yet he gave him heaven and earth. He gave him heaven without promising it, the earth without undertaking to, and paradise and everything else. What he never promised, he gave. Will he not give what he promised with a guarantee?

Scripture calls the gospel sometimes a new covenant, sometimes a young covenant, sometimes a better covenant, sometimes a second, sometimes an eternal one. Since one name cannot express its whole power, Scripture shows the power of the gospel by various names. Paul especially, who had Christ speaking in him, calls the gospel a new covenant because it renews the old. For "new" denotes something strange and truly untouched. "Young" is in contrast with what has grown old, "better" with what is inferior, "second" with what is first, and "eternal" with what is temporary.

It is called a new covenant according to blessed Jeremiah, who says, "And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord, that I will make a new covenant with you." And the Savior, when he handed down the mystery, says, "This is my body, the body of the new covenant." There is the new covenant.

Elsewhere he calls it young, because the preaching is young and in its prime. Paul says, "We have come to Mount Zion, to myriads of angels, to the assembly of the firstborn, and to Jesus, the mediator of a young covenant." By saying "new" he has made the first one old.

Elsewhere he calls it a better covenant, saying, "But now we have obtained a more excellent ministry, just as he is mediator of a better covenant. For if the first had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second." There you have both first and second.

Where is "eternal"? Listen to Paul saying, "Now the God of peace, who brought up from the earth the great shepherd of the sheep by the blood of the eternal covenant." Since the first covenant was temporary, this one is eternal. And elsewhere it says, "I will make an eternal covenant with you, the holy and sure mercies of David." New covenant, young, first, second, better, eternal: Jesus is the guarantor of these covenants.

So when man is about to be renewed, heaven becomes new. It is not destroyed but renewed together with the new creation. The sun is new, the moon new, the stars new, receiving increase and growth. For the prophet says, "The heaven shall be new and the earth new." See, creation is renewed, and the one who promised does not lie. As much increase as man receives, the elements also receive. How do we know this? Isaiah says, "For the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, and the light of the moon shall be like the sun." Do you see how God did not break his promise, but renewed creation? And the author of the renewal is Christ.

The offspring of heretics took up this idea and put forward the words "Firstborn of all creation." They do not understand that it speaks not of the creation that came into being but of the creation that is being renewed.

What is the creation that is being renewed? Hear Paul saying: "If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." And to show that Christ is called firstborn of the creation that is being renewed, he adds: "The firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might have the first place." He has the first place among those who are being renewed, among those called to incorruption, among those raised from the dead. "In all things having the first place": not according to his Godhead, for it is an insult to God to be called "first", an insult that passes for honour. In the divine and uncreated nature there is no first and second. Everything there has a living beginning, a beginning without beginning, an eternal beginning, incomprehensible and inexpressible. But among things of our order Christ has the first place, whether compared with Paul or compared with Peter. Empty would be our hope, vain would be our hope, if Christ ranked first over these in his Godhead. No, he ranks first in his humanity, as the one who renewed Adam and gave life to the world. That is why he says: "The firstborn from the dead, so that in all things he might have the first place."

And how is he "firstborn from the dead"? Let us look into this, I beg you. For if I pass over the word without examining it, the soul, being inquisitive, puts forward its own objections and thinks them strong. "How," it asks, "is Christ the firstborn of the dead, when even before his coming Elijah raised the widow's son, and Elisha raised the son of the Shunammite woman, and the Saviour himself raised Lazarus, the daughter of Jairus, and the widow's son? If, then, the dead were raised both in the Old Testament and in the New, how is Christ the firstborn of the dead?"

What then? Even if those people rose before Christ, all of them died again after rising; they gave only a foretaste of the resurrection. But Christ, having risen, is no longer subject to death. That is why he is the pioneer: he rose and dies no more. And Paul says: "For Christ, having been raised from the dead, dies no more; death no longer has dominion over him." Do you see him who has the first place in all things? Do you see him who renews our race through his own dispensation? In the end he drew humanity up, brought it into heaven, and seated it at the right hand of God.

O our wicked and foolish heart! Christ came to us; he gave us the Spirit that is from him, and he took up our body. The exchange was made, and ingratitude insults the benefit. He took from us what was fashioned, and sat down at the right hand of God. We received from him the Spirit, and have we insulted it by dragging it down to the rank of a creature and a servant? O wretched and miserable man! What if Christ says to you on that day: "I honoured your body with immortality, and you dragged my Spirit down to the nature of a creature"? You saw what was mortal raised up; you saw it sharing the throne; you saw it above every rule and authority and dominion. And are you not ashamed? God honours what is ours, and do we not honour what is his?

But I know that heretical wickedness wages war on the truth. "I know," it says, "that this body was taken up into heaven, but not so much in order to be honoured as so that we might have an advocate above, who entreats God on our behalf." This is why shameless tongues and untaught souls used to say in the marketplace, making a public show of holy things… I do not know how to put it, for I will not repeat the wording of the blasphemy, but I will restate its sense: "You, Christ," they say, "pray to God for us and intercede for us." And they take a saying of the apostle without having learned its meaning. "Did not the apostle say," they ask, "'Christ who died, or rather who was also raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us'? Did we invent this? Did we falsify divine things? Paul said that Christ intercedes for us."

They have not paid attention to what intercession is, nor seen that there is a great difference between supplication and intercession. If interceding and entreating were the same thing, Paul would not have said: "I want you to offer prayers, supplications, intercessions and thanksgivings." It is called supplication when someone entreats God for something. It is called prayer when one sings God's praises. It is called thanksgiving when someone gives thanks to God for the good he has received. It is called intercession when someone appeals to God against wrongdoers, calling on him to avenge. That interceding is not pleading, but questioning and receiving an answer, the Old Testament bears witness when it says: "And God said to Elijah the prophet: What are you doing here, Elijah?" God questions the prophet, and the prophet answers: "I have been very zealous for the Lord Almighty, because the children of Israel have forsaken you. They have torn down your altars and killed your prophets with the sword, and I alone am left, and they seek my life." There was no supplication here, no prayer, but question and answer, and this was an intercession. How so? Hear Paul saying: "Or do you not know what the Scripture says of Elijah the prophet, how he intercedes with God against Israel?" So intercession is not supplication. It is the forceful protest of a prophet reporting to God the outrages that have been committed.

Since, then, the apostles were in danger among the nations, dragged before rulers and governors and plotted against by the Jews, and the apostle was preparing them to scorn everything—persecution, affliction and death—he says, as if to console them: "Even if you say nothing against those who wrong you, there is one who intercedes for you, the one who took his human form from you. Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies; who is the one who condemns? It is Christ who died, or rather who was also raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us."
If he intercedes, how is he seated? Does not one who intercedes stand to do so? Have you ever seen anyone interceding like a servant while sitting at the ruler's right hand?

But this is why, he says, he puts the dignity first, saying: "Who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us." It is as if he were saying: "You have no need to worry about anything that happens. Attend to preaching virtue. Do not distract yourself by saying: 'Lord, how much we suffer! We are driven out, we are persecuted.' You have one who speaks for you there; you have one who intercedes." And the Son intercedes with the Father, not in a subordinate rank, but as a son telling his father how things stand: "Those who believe in us are wronged, persecuted, driven out." To make the accusation credible, he brings in the Son as the one who intercedes. So too the Saviour says: "Or do you think that I will accuse you? The one who accuses you is Moses, in whom you have set your hope." Is the Son lesser, in your view, because he intercedes with the Father? Then if you see God interceding with a man against the unfaithful, what will you do? Hear the Lord saying to Jeremiah: "Have you seen what the senseless daughter of Judah has done to me? She has forsaken me and gone after other gods." Very well: a man intercedes with God. But why does God intercede with a man? And elsewhere: "And now, you men of Judah and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, judge between me and my vineyard. What more ought I to have done that I have not done?"

So it is with Christ. While he was fulfilling the dispensation in the flesh, he was a priest; he offered supplications and prayed to the Father, in keeping with his dispensation in the flesh. But since he ascended into heaven he simply sits in glory, not pleading, not interceding. Or if he does intercede, he does so as a son with his father, just as God also interceded with a prophet. This is why Paul, to show that Christ does not stand above like a priest offering sacrifice for himself and for the people, but is seated, says: "For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest, who sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high, who has no need, as the priest does, to offer sacrifice day by day for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered up himself."

Why, then, do they rage against true religion? If he had no need, do you put under necessity the one who is above all necessity? Again Paul adds: "For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made with hands, a copy of the true one, but into heaven itself, to appear in the presence of God on our behalf." He did not say "to be continually appearing"; for he appeared once, not many times. And again: "Nor was it to offer himself hour by hour, as the priest enters the Holy of Holies once a year. But now Christ has appeared once for all to do away with sin by the sacrifice of himself. And the other priests stand daily at their service, offering the same sacrifices; but Christ, having offered a single sacrifice for sins, sat down for ever, waiting until his enemies are put under his feet." Does he still intercede, then? He is seated. Why do you insult the benefit he has given?

But I know that I have drawn out my discourse at length. Forgive me: I entered the deep, and by the power of the Holy Spirit I was able to swim across the sea of the holy Scriptures—not so as to say what is worthy of them, but as far as we were able. But above all I urge you and beg you, and I will not stop begging you: search the Scriptures, seek the truth, learn about Christ from Christ. Do not surrender yourself to heretical wickedness. The devil has many serpents today in place of the ancient serpent. He sows the tares of sin so as to reap the ruin of impiety. Do not, I beg you! Let us wall off our ears against heretical wickedness.

I know I have said this to you before, but I say it now as well: the founders of every heresy are well known. From Arius come the Arians, from Macedonius the Macedonians, from Eunomius the Eunomians, from Marcion the Marcionites, from Sabellius the Sabellians, from Mani the Manichaeans, from Montanus the Montanists, and so on through the rest of the heresies. If the faith of the Church is heretical, let the heretics say who its founder is. Let them say: "Your heresy began with such-and-such a man." Let them say it, if they know. See how good God has been in this. God did not allow a man's name to be attached to the glory of the apostles. We are not called Macedonians; and even if they call us "Homoousians", they have not named a man, but have shown the harmony of our faith. If, then, you ask them, "And who first said 'homoousios'?", they cannot say "So-and-so and so-and-so." No, three hundred and eighteen fathers, raising a single harmonious voice of confession, agreed together in true religion.

Notice how the confession of virtue itself shines out. The homoousios was not begun by one man, nor by two, but by a whole synod from east, west, south and north; for where the truth appears, everything agrees. Ask a heretic what I am about to tell you. If you ask an orthodox believer, even an unlearned and inexperienced one, he says this: "I confess Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one kingdom, one power." But say to two or three heretics, "What do you believe?" If they arrive at the same words, they are telling the truth. But one says "Uncreated", another "Begotten", another "Immortal", another "Eternal". And if yet another pops up, he says: "I know that the Father made the Son, and the Son made everything else." Then another corrects him, saying: "Not so. The Father made the Son, and through the Son all things came into being." For where there is no truth, the garment is rotten and it tears. And just as, brothers, a worn-out garment tears wherever it snags, and even if you draw someone into conversation by its appearance [?], its rottenness is exposed and it tears at the slightest occasion, so it is with the heresies: one confesses one thing, another something else.

Foreign heresies, foreign names—and disgraceful ones at that, names taken from petty tradesmen! The heretics have suffered what the Jews once suffered. Under the law the holy lampstand stood in the Holy of Holies, where the veil was, where the table was, where the law was, where the tablets were. Since they fell away from the truth, where does the lampstand stand? In the doorways of taverns. Where is the horn of the prophets? In the taverns. And they do this not out of devotion but for profit, not to show the lampstand being honoured, but to call in passers-by and show them that the wine is Jewish. Just as there the holy things, held by the unworthy, were brought down from the sanctuary to such cheapness, so here too: from Paul and Peter, from that summit—I am ashamed to say it, I blush at the name of the disgrace; truly I blush even to speak of it, yet I am forced to speak—after that saying, "You are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it," after Paul said, "If you seek proof of Christ speaking in me"—after Paul and Peter, after the evangelists, the heralds and the confessors, people are now called Psathyrians and suchlike names.

When have they ever kept their shape? When has the worn-out garment not torn apart? But I will end my discourse by applying to them the prophet's words: "They were torn apart and were not pierced with remorse." Here, by contrast, the tunic of the Church is woven in one piece throughout, without seam. Why does it say "woven"? Because many things are made from pieces stuck together. But this tunic was not pieced together from human reasonings; it is from above, woven in one piece throughout, without seam. It was not human reasonings that stitched our faith together; we have the tunic whole.

We have fulfilled our promise, which was a large one, intricate and subtle in its reflection. Let the hearer understand that simple thoughts use simple words, but deep reflections need great variety. When you meet an obscure saying, lift up your mind; when you meet a subtle thought, make your mind supple. Many of God's sayings are brief, such as "You shall not murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness." But when he says, "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us," and "After this he appeared on earth and lived among men," the garment is many-coloured, as it is written: "the manifold wisdom of God."

For all these things let us glorify him who appeared, worship him who came, and sing the praises of him who renewed us, who gave us life, who raised us up, who walled us round, who enlightened us, who has freely given us an abundance of every good thing: Christ Jesus, to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, to the ages of ages. Amen.
